---
title: "Roadmap"
subtitle: "What v2.1 does now, and what comes next."
---

## Done in the first pass

- [x] Value Added v2.0 specified on the review's recommendations and fitted
      for all, disadvantaged, non-disadvantaged pupils, girls and boys
- [x] Value added against England and within the authority, shrunk, with
      95% intervals
- [x] Every school in England, explored by region, combined or mayoral authority, or local authority, on a map with a sortable table, and a downloadable file
- [x] Pages for Sussex, its three authorities and twelve districts, with the
      map, the girls/boys split, a v2.0 decomposition and the latest Ofsted
      judgement
- [x] Comparison with the published v1 measure throughout
- [x] Absence above or below what the intake predicts, on the v2 intake
      terms, on every map and in every profile
- [x] The original Sussex documents' analyses refitted on v2.0: the
      decomposition, the district test, trusts, the joint-signal plane,
      absence scenarios, comparator profiles, league tables and questions
      for discussion; a district summary page
- [x] Value added over time: every school's yearly v2.0 value added,
      trajectories in the explorer and on every area page, and a centred
      moving average over one, three or five years around a chosen year

## Done since: absence, schools and twins {#done-absence}

- [x] **What goes with school absence.** [A page](absence_causes.qmd) that
      starts from a map of the UK research (with links to the sources),
      shows the trend by reason since 2016/17, and models seven kinds of
      absence in 2025/26 on every secondary school's intake, needs and
      setting, with each school nested in its authority and region. Shapley
      shares say how much each group of characteristics explains, and the
      full models (coefficients, random effects, fit) are on the page.
- [x] **The school's part.** What the models attribute to "the school" is
      mostly selection through admissions; what is left between similar
      schools is wide and lasts from one year to the next. A message for
      heads and governors, nationally and on every area page.
- [x] **Absence on every Sussex page.** Each authority's and district's
      absence against England, its neighbours and the tier above, what in
      its intake raises or lowers it, and its schools against similar
      schools in both years.
- [x] **[Find a twin](twins.qmd).** Choose a school and find the schools in
      England most like it in intake and setting, or the look-alikes that do
      better on absence, attainment or value added, on a chart and a map,
      with fact cards side by side. Linked from the absence page and every
      area page, and every comparison has its own link.
- [x] **[How school absence changes](absence_change.qmd)** (started).
      Every secondary school followed from 2016/17 to 2025/26 through
      academy conversion and changes of trust: what is lasting and what
      moves, whether schools keep their place, who rose most since the
      pandemic, whether absence moves when a school's own intake does, and
      event studies of becoming an academy and of a change of trust.
- [x] **The explorer.** Ofsted colours that work across both inspection
      regimes, in each palette, and the spread of schools on the map
      beneath it, as on the Sussex pages.

## Next

- [x] **Policy simulator v2.0.** The Pull the Right Lever
      simulator rebuilt on the v2.1 models: absence and the
      intake terms as levers (with admissions and sixth form for one
      school), all five groups at once with the disadvantage gap, each
      lever's contribution, and an area mode that applies a change to every
      school in an area. First in the browser, now part of the School
      Information System below.
- [x] **[School Information System v2.0](simulator.qmd) (Shiny).** The v1.0 policy simulator
      app rebuilt on v2.1, on Posit Connect Cloud (`app/`): Attainment 8 and
      value added side by side for all, disadvantaged and non-disadvantaged
      pupils; four years, single years or moving averages; regions,
      combined authorities, authorities, districts and trusts; absence
      against expected; a school finder, twins, observed against predicted,
      the simulator, an area overview, and travel and distance with the
      national walking routes as they arrive. It replaces the site's
      in-browser simulator.
- [x] **[Pupil numbers and school places](demographics.qmd).** Pupils by
      year group in every local authority since 2015/16, which areas are in
      consistent decline or growth, the cohorts in school rolled forward to
      Year 7 in 2032/33, and every state mainstream school opened, closed or
      merged since 2015/16 on a map.
- [x] **[School finances before closure](finance.qmd).** Every state
      school that closed or merged since 2017/18 followed through its
      finance returns (CFR from 2014-15, academies' AAR from 2016-17):
      rolls fall first, money follows; a model of closure within two (and
      two to three) years tested on later years; five simple warning signs;
      and counts of open schools showing them by authority, with no open
      school named.
- [x] **[School Information System v2.1](simulator.qmd).** Two new tabs:
      Pupils and Places (pupils by year group, the Year 7 roll-forward,
      openings and closures, for any authority, region or England) and
      School Finances (deficits, reserves, income per pupil and warning-sign
      counts, by authority, region and Sussex district, no school named);
      and walking catchments for every state secondary now that the national
      routing is complete (`R/46_app_v21_data.R`).
- [ ] **Still to come on places:** school capacity and surplus places
      (SCAP), and how each school's intake is changing, beside its value
      added.
- [ ] **Do schools push up house prices? A national test.** It is often said that
      homes near the most popular schools cost 20 to 25% more. Tan and Dennett
      found in Brighton (81,652 sales, 2000 to 2019) that, once the home and its
      neighbourhood are accounted for, a good school nearby adds only a few per
      cent, and that the 2008 admissions lottery made no difference.
    - **The national version:** every sale in England, with its floor area and
      rooms from Chris Beech's fast
      [Price Paid to EPC linkage](https://github.com/chris-beech-housing/Land-Registry-PPD-EPC-price-per-square-metre),
      after Chi et al.
    - **Linked to schools** by walking time through the national routing, and to
      each school's Ofsted grade, value added and popularity at the date of sale.
    - **Tests:** the raw premium first, then with neighbourhood effects, then
      changes in Ofsted grade or value added over time.
    - **For the first time at this scale:** whether buyers pay for value added
      or for intake.
- [ ] **Brighton and Hove: why are numbers falling?** Fertility in the city is
      0.98 children per woman (2025), the 2nd lowest of 292 districts. Neither
      the fall since 2015 nor the low level follows affordability: neighbouring
      Lewes, Mid Sussex and Wealden have the same house price to earnings ratio
      but fertility of 1.45 to 1.58 (`R/49`). Births, not families moving out,
      drive most of the city's fall in primary pupils (`R/50`), while in inner
      London migration matters as much. Next: write this up, and test whether
      women's education (Census Level 4+) explains low fertility better than
      housing costs.
- [ ] **School Information System v2.2: primary and post-16.** The same view
      for primary schools, then sixth forms and colleges (placeholders in
      the app).
- [ ] **Adding a new year.** When DfE publishes a new year's KS4 results,
      add it to `YEAR_CONFIG` in `pipeline/helpers.R`, run
      `R/00_fetch_data.R`, then the build steps. The v2.1 model takes its
      years from the data, and no longer needs the workforce file, which
      was the slowest to arrive. See the README.
- [x] **A self-contained data pipeline for the model.** `R/00_fetch_data.R`
      builds every model input from public sources (DfE, GIAS, ONS, nomis,
      postcodes.io, Ofsted), with the scripts in `pipeline/`. Rebuilt from
      the same downloads it reproduces the inputs, and every value-added
      figure, exactly.
- [ ] **The Sussex area analyses, self-contained too.** The area pages
      still reuse the original project's area analyses (a snapshot in
      `data/area/`), its Sussex governance and its absence reasons. Port
      its R/15, R/17 and R/19 next.
- [ ] **Update 2025/26 with the revised KS4 release (February 2027).**
      2025/26 is shown now, provisional, predicted from the fitted model on
      DfE's October results with absence bridged and the unpublished intake
      data carried forward (`R/05_provisional_2526.R`). Rerun it on the
      revised results; then, once the year's census, SEN and mobility data
      are out, fold 2025/26 into the model as a fifth year.
- [x] **v2.1 candidates tested across every group:** the illness share of
      absence and an 11–16 flag ([the methodology](method.qmd#sec-v21)),
      with a chart of what matters most in the model.
- [x] **v2.1 published.** The 11–16 flag is in the expectation (a school's
      structure, like its admissions policy). Value added allowing for the
      kind of absence is published beside it, not in it, because what is
      authorised as illness is partly a school's own coding.
- [x] **[Neighbourhood types (OAC)](neighbourhood_types.qmd).** The 2021/2
      Output Area Classification profiled over each school's 150 nearest
      Output Areas at all three tiers. It reproduces neighbourhood education,
      adds nothing to results or to value added within authorities, and
      describes the places behind the authority effects for disadvantaged
      pupils (multicultural urban areas above, small-town, coastal and
      former industrial areas below). Groups are enough; subgroups add little.
- [x] **[Geographical effects across England](geography.qmd).** How much of
      value added is region and local authority, for every group; a map of
      the authority effects; region averages; and what goes with them.
- [x] **[Neighbourhood covariates](neighbourhood_covariates.qmd) (experiment).**
      Ten Census 2021 measures and each school's own White British share
      added to v2.1. For disadvantaged pupils, the ethnic pattern is mostly
      composition (pupils, not place); neighbourhood deprivation beyond
      qualifications is place. Together they take about a fifth off the
      authority effects and over a third off the regional ones for
      disadvantaged pupils; about a third of Brighton and Hove's effect.
- [x] **[v2.2 candidates](v22.qmd) tested across every group and year.**
      Neighbourhood household deprivation helps every group in every year
      (recommended for v2.2). Pupils' ethnicity (school White British share,
      each January) matters almost only for disadvantaged pupils, where it
      is large; recommended beside the headline, not in it.
- [ ] **Value Added v2.2 (agreed, for a future release).** The approach
      from the [v2.2 candidates](v22.qmd) is agreed but not yet built:
      refit every group with neighbourhood household deprivation in the
      expectation beside neighbourhood education; publish value added
      allowing for pupils' ethnicity beside the headline, labelled, not in
      it; and before release, test detailed ethnic groups rather than the
      White British share alone. Until then the site publishes v2.1.
- [x] **[Parents, not adults](neighbourhood_covariates.qmd#sec-parents).**
      Neighbourhood education rebuilt from custom Census tables as graduates
      among parents (adults 25-64 with dependent children, MSOA). All-adult
      graduate shares hide a 12-point gap in parents between deprived and
      comfortable graduate-rich neighbourhoods, and the young-adult penalty
      almost disappears. Parents alone is no better a term; parents and other
      adults together help every group a little. Deprivation survives.
- [ ] **v2.2 candidate: split neighbourhood education** into parents and
      other adults, and follow up why disadvantaged pupils do better near
      graduates without children.
- [ ] **What causes school-level absence, continued.** The cross-section
      and change over time are under way ([above](#done-absence)). Next:
      each school's own path relative to England on the area pages and in
      Find a twin, whether high-illness places such as Brighton and Hove
      record absence differently, the severe tail on its own, whether
      particular trusts' schools move together, and absence against intake
      by kind as a candidate for a future version of the model.
- [x] **Twins, further.** The matching is weighted by what matters for the
      measure chosen (equal weights still available), the fact cards show
      value added and absence year by year against the twin and England,
      and a comparison prints cleanly for a governors' meeting.
- [x] **[Distance to school](distance.qmd): the straight-line check.** The
      distance from every neighbourhood in England to its nearest state
      secondary, by deprivation, in every district and authority. Across
      England deprived neighbourhoods are usually nearer; in Brighton and
      Hove they are about a third further away. Absence goes with distance
      by authority, more for disadvantaged pupils, and by school, mostly in
      illness and persistent absence. It builds on
      [FFT Education Datalab's finding](https://ffteducationdatalab.org.uk/2023/11/are-pupils-who-live-further-away-from-their-school-absent-more-often/)
      that pupils who live further away are absent more often.
- [x] **[How firm is the link with absence?](distance.qmd#sec-firm)** Six
      years, eleven measures of distance and thousands of models for all three
      groups of pupils, a falsification test on primary absence, DfE's absence
      by home neighbourhood within each authority, and changes in the school
      network. The link is consistent and stronger for disadvantaged pupils,
      but most of its size between authorities is ethnic mix; a smaller link
      remains in towns and cities, within authorities and between schools.
      Every source and calculation is in
      [the methodology](method.qmd#sec-distance-method).
- [x] **[Journey times on the real networks](distance.qmd#sec-journeys).**
      Walking and bus times with r5r from every Output Area in Brighton and
      Hove and eight comparator places, with changes of bus, the penalty for
      missing a journey, school buses and the climb each way. Brighton and Hove
      stands out on real journeys as it does in straight lines. None of these
      shows a clear general link with absence yet; Longhill stands out on
      missing the bus.
- [x] **[Journey times for the 109 mostly urban authorities](distance.qmd#sec-la-journeys).**
      Every Output Area routed on 28 networks, London included (buses only).
      No authority's deprived neighbourhoods are as far from a school as
      Brighton and Hove's, mostly because of distance, and they need the most
      changes of bus. Time does not beat straight-line distance for absence,
      and changes, waits and missing a bus add nothing once distance is known.
      The climb is the one feature that keeps appearing.
- [x] **[Points of interest around bus changes and along walking routes](distance.qmd#sec-la-poi).**
      From OpenStreetMap, in five groups. Nothing across authorities; within
      authorities a hint that busier change points go with more secondary
      absence, mostly in London, where bus-only routes are least like real
      journeys.
- [x] **[What it could mean for GCSE results](distance.qmd#sec-gcse).**
      Distance carried through absence to Attainment 8, a direct check, and
      Gorard and Siddiqui's mixing estimate on the same scale.
- [x] **[What Brighton and Hove's admissions changes did](distance.qmd#sec-admissions).**
      From the city's school system model: the 2024 map and priority 6
      lengthened disadvantaged children's journeys by well under a minute and
      lowered segregation a little. Both are worth a fraction of an
      Attainment 8 point; where the schools are matters far more.
- [x] **[The proposals that did not go ahead](distance.qmd#sec-proposals).**
      The council's 2024 proposal (priority 6 at 20%, Stringer and
      Blatchington Mill at 300) and Class Divide's (30%, with the cuts), run on the published
      model: longer journeys and more children displaced, no gain in mixing,
      and nothing more from 30% than from 20%.
- [x] **[Whose journeys changed most](distance.qmd#sec-admissions-neighbourhoods).**
      Neighbourhood by neighbourhood: the 2024 map lengthened journeys from
      Whitehawk by about three minutes, more for its disadvantaged children,
      while the city average barely moved.
- [x] **[A trust view: Aldridge Education](trust_aldridge.qmd).** The
      trust's eight secondary schools on value added, attendance, intake and
      place, with targets that start from each school's intake, the levers
      most likely to help (attendance, subject areas, staffing), and similar
      schools doing well on each to talk to. Any trust can be run by name.
- [ ] **Rail, Metro and trams.** Timetables beyond the Bus Open Data Service,
      for London and the large conurbations.
- [ ] **School bells.** Published start times for each school, in place of the
      time inferred from the last school bus, for the penalty for missing one.
- [ ] **Distance to school: how far each school's pupils travel.** A better
      measure than each school's nearest children, such as a gravity model
      of who goes where, built from published sources.
- [ ] **Distance to school: does it matter more in towns and cities?** The
      hypothesis: distance matters for attendance more than is understood,
      and may matter *more* in towns and cities, where a longer journey
      passes more places to stop on the way (intervening opportunities),
      than in rural areas, where long journeys are the norm and often by
      school transport. [Between authorities](distance.qmd#sec-urban) the
      link is strong in mostly urban places and absent in less urban ones,
      but within authorities and by school it is similar in both, so it needs
      journey times and data on school transport.
- [x] **[Independent schools](independent.qmd).** What is published for
      them, term by term against v2.1; why their Attainment 8 cannot be
      compared (IGCSEs score nothing, and KS4 and A level results are
      unrelated); a test showing a reduced specification gets value added
      badly wrong even in the state sector; and the comparison that does
      exist, DfE's A level value added. Verdict: no value added at 16 is
      possible from published data.
- [x] **Independent schools: IGCSEs.** DfE's 16-19 guidance checked: A level
      value added counts approved GCSEs only, so IGCSEs are left out of the
      baseline (most independent students still have some GCSEs). Attainment
      8 completed from its published parts: the average grade in counting
      GCSEs, validated on state schools (R² 0.88-0.90) and against
      independent schools' own A level results (r 0.84, against 0.03).
- [ ] **Independent schools, next.** A level value added over three years
      and by subject; the completed Attainment 8 over several years; and the
      two sectors' sixth forms side by side by area.
- [ ] **Areas beyond Sussex.** The area template works for any authority
      and its districts once boundaries are added.
- [x] **Monthly Ofsted refresh.** A GitHub Actions workflow picks up
      Ofsted's new release on the 20th of each month, updates every
      school's latest judgement without refitting, rerenders and commits.
- [ ] **Publish v2.1 alongside v1** in the original reports, labelled, with
      a note on how rankings change.
